extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and working stand-up comedians (performers learning craft and club-level pros)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for stand-up comedians on handling bombing, hecklers, and turning bad gigs into material and skill improvements. Focuses on mindset, practical exercises (recording/reviewing), and preparing comebacks/tools for hostile or unreceptive audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that everybody bombs
rubrics_metrics.description: Bombing is a normal part of a stand-up career; 'Everybody Bombs!' and having a bad gig doesn't mean much long-term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post emphasizes mindset: bombing happens to all comics at some point and the humiliation is short-lived. Use the experience rather than letting it end your career. Example language: 'Whether you have bombed or not doesn’t mean anything. What you do with that experience defines your character.'

rubrics_metrics.name: One gig isn't decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: That one gig that feels important in the moment 'isn’t. It’s just one gig.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't treat a single poor performance as career-ending. Perspective reduces humiliation and enables learning. The post repeats that the significance of one bad show is limited and that long-term progress matters more than isolated failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze recordings of your set
rubrics_metrics.description: Record your performance and review it closely: 'I turned around, grabbed my recorder ... It’s my black box. It recorded everything that led up to the crash.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete exercise: listen to every line audience members and you said, transcribe them, and use that material to generate responses and improvements. Recording enables objective analysis rather than relying on memory or emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a toolbox of comebacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Write and rehearse many comeback lines and responses you can use when being heckled or when a bit isn't working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author wrote 'like thirty comebacks' after the bad gig; this produced usable lines that can be deployed later. Example comeback provided in the post illustrates a sharp, provocative retort. The guidance implies practicing these so they're ready under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for and manage hecklers
rubrics_metrics.description: Have strategies and practiced lines for tag-team heckling and audience members who 'go fuck with' a struggling comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rusty Pelican story describes 'tag team heckling' and shows the need for prepared responses. Anti-pattern: freezing, saying weak filler ('At least you can enjoy the music'), or walking off without an effective retort. The post advises building specific responses and tools to handle this scenario.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not escalate physically or retaliate violently
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist impulses to respond to hecklers with violence or threats: the author considered breaking a beer bottle but recognized practical and legal consequences and that it was a cowardly impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical and ethical reasons to avoid physical retaliation: loss of bookings, jail, reputation damage. Instead, channel emotion into productive preparation and learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor material to venue and audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some venues/audiences aren't expecting comedy (e.g., band breaks at restaurants) and are among 'the worst gigs you can do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid or adapt material for contexts where comedy isn't expected or the audience makeup will make certain topics inappropriate. The post notes performing during a band's break in a restaurant is especially challenging because 'nobody expects comedy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Match material culturally and demographically to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid performing culturally inappropriate material for a given audience (commenter example: a Jewish comic should not perform Latino humor for a 95% Latino crowd).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the comments: learn audience composition and sensibilities before trying material tied to other cultures or identities. Anti-pattern: alienating the crowd by using culturally misplaced jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mistakes as a source of growth—apply solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Embrace mistakes, find solutions to the problems they reveal, and apply those solutions to improve craft: 'We take our biggest leaps from our biggest mistakes ... only if we embrace them, find solutions ... and apply the solutions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific actions include analyzing recordings, writing new material/responses, practicing delivery, and incorporating lessons into future performances. The goal is to come out 'sharper, smarter and faster.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain persistence and keep performing
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t quit after bombing; many comics who bomb may stop performing, but persistence is key to a career in comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post contrasts comics who never step on stage again with the author's decision to keep working. Persistence allows accumulation of tools and experience; the Rusty Pelican incident ultimately contributed to the author's development and long-term success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop strong stage presence and confidence independent of immediate laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a set bombs, elements like 'stage presence' can be defensible and are sometimes noted by peers; but stage presence alone doesn't substitute for workable material and responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post references post-gig comments such as 'That was brave' or 'At least you had good stage presence' as common reactions. Use presence, but focus on building material and responses so presence supports, not masks, the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice writing and testing material repeatedly
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterate on jokes and test them in different settings; the author practiced by performing short sets during band breaks and then refined lines afterward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even suboptimal practice contexts provide opportunities to try lines and learn. The author used poor gigs as data points to write and refine many comebacks and bits.
